questions.q: In the structural analogy between QNNs and classical neural networks, what plays the role of a 'linear layer,' and what has no classical analogue at all?
options: Parameterized rotation layers loosely play the 'weights' role; entangling layers (like CNOT) have no classical neural-network analogue
Entangling layers play the weights role; rotation layers have no classical analogue
Both rotation and entangling layers map perfectly onto classical activation functions
Neither layer type has any relationship to classical neural network components
questions.explain: Parameterized rotation layers are loosely analogous to a linear layer's trainable weights, while entangling layers introduce correlations between qubits with no direct classical neural-network counterpart.

questions.q: What is the real distinction between the terms 'QNN' and 'VQC' as used in this lesson?
options: A difference of architectural emphasis and naming convention -- QNN usually implies a deeper stack of layers by analogy to classical depth, not a different underlying training algorithm
QNNs use entirely different training algorithms than VQCs, with no parameter-shift gradients involved
VQCs can only be used for regression, while QNNs can only be used for classification
QNN refers exclusively to quantum hardware implementations, while VQC refers exclusively to simulations
questions.explain: Both use the identical encode-ansatz-measure-loss-gradient-update loop; the QNN label is typically reserved for deeper layer stacks explicitly motivated by analogy to classical network depth, not a structurally different algorithm.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say 'quantum neuron' proposals (e.g., repeat-until-success circuits) are NOT the dominant approach used in practical QML work today?
options: The layered rotation+entangling ansatz is what's actually used in PennyLane/Qiskit ML tutorials, papers, and labs -- quantum neuron constructs exist in the literature but aren't the mainstream practical approach
Quantum neuron proposals have been mathematically proven impossible to implement on any hardware
Quantum neuron proposals were the original basis for all of Chapter 2's parameter-shift rule content
Quantum neurons require fewer qubits than any other QNN approach, making them strictly preferable
questions.explain: While quantum-neuron constructs are a real, named research thread worth knowing, the layered rotation+entangling ansatz is what dominates actual practical usage in libraries and this course's labs.

questions.q: Why is there no natural quantum-gate analogue of a classical nonlinear activation function like ReLU?
options: Quantum states evolve linearly (unitarily) between measurements, so there is no built-in gate that introduces the kind of nonlinearity activation functions provide classically
Quantum gates are inherently nonlinear, making an activation function redundant and unnecessary
Nonlinear activation functions have already been fully implemented as standard quantum gates in every major QML library
This is purely a software limitation of PennyLane and Qiskit, not a physical constraint
questions.explain: Quantum mechanics evolves states linearly/unitarily between measurements -- there's no natural quantum gate behaving like a classical nonlinear activation, which is a genuine physical/mathematical constraint, not a software gap.

questions.q: What is incomplete about claiming a 10-layer QNN is 'strictly more powerful' than a 1-layer VQC the same way a 10-layer classical network beats a 1-layer one?
options: Classical depth gains power specifically because of stacked nonlinear activations between linear layers; quantum circuits lack a clean equivalent, so depth doesn't translate into expressiveness gains the same way, and also worsens barren plateau risk
Nothing is incomplete; the comparison is exactly correct and transfers directly
A 1-layer VQC is always mathematically identical to a 10-layer QNN regardless of design
Classical neural networks never actually benefit from depth, making the comparison irrelevant either way
questions.explain: Classical depth's power comes from nonlinear activations between linear layers -- a mechanism quantum circuits don't cleanly have. Meanwhile, the extra depth of a QNN actively worsens barren-plateau risk (Lesson 8), so more layers isn't a straightforward win the way it can be classically.
